title: Norway’s Telenor telecom faces lawsuit for giving user data to Myanmar junta
content:
The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Norway-based multinational telecom company Telenor is facing charges for its role in turning over sensitive customer data to the military government of Myanmar.

If successful, the case would be the first ever to hold a telecom company accountable for failing to protect user data from being misused by an authoritarian regime.
snippet:
The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity

title: When free speech has a price: Youth voices in Mozambique
content:
When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

A group of men during a peaceful protest; one of them holds a microphone and a banner. Photo taken by Stephanie Douglas. Nigeria. Via Pexels. Pexels License.

In Mozambique, freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014, a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique. However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience.
snippet:
When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence

title: Trump’s ‘Agreements on Reciprocal Trade’ (ARTs) threaten equitable access to the internet in Global South
content:
The provision could give the U.S. the power to exclude Chinese ICT suppliers in signatory countries

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Image remix on Canva by Ihsan Kamil/EngageMedia. Used with permission.

This article, written by Prapasiri “Nan” Suttisome, was first published by EngageMedia, a non-profit media, technology, and culture organization, and an edited version is republished here as part of a content-sharing agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Around the world, one in every three people has no reliable access to the internet. Unequal access to the internet creates digital divides that can limit civic participation, undermine access to education and healthcare, and deepen inequality. It can also reduce innovation, industrial growth, and economic output. Reducing digital divides is recognized as essential for progress on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals, as reaffirmed by the more recent Global Digital Compact, 2024.
snippet:
The provision could give the U.S. the power to exclude Chinese ICT suppliers in signatory countries

title: Africa’s governments already treat the internet as protest infrastructure. Its courts have not caught up
content:
When many people gather, some states are not prosecuting people. Instead, it cuts the network

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Kenya Judiciary building.  Image by Wing via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

On a Saturday in late July 2025, Angola shut down its internet for the first time in its recorded history. Not during an election, and not during a war. People had taken to the streets to protest the rising price of fuel. At least 22 people were killed according to the authorities’ own figures; civil society monitors counted 30 dead and more than 1,500 arrested.
snippet:
When many people gather, some states are not prosecuting people. Instead, it cuts the network

title: Subsea cables and oil pipelines: The infrastructure linking AI, empire, and occupation
content:
Internet infrastructure policy is increasingly a topic of discussion in military strategy and policy decision-making

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Screenshot of the Internet Infrastructure Map in 2026, from kmcd.dev. Fair use

By Alli Armijo

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The internet has always been illusive. Stretching bodies of water, screens, and time zones, it exists in a plurality increasingly shaped by big tech. And the cables mediate this; the cables are its nervous system.

With over 600 active and planned underwater internet cables spanning over 1.5 million kilometers around the globe, the majority of subsea infrastructure is predominantly owned and operated by US tech monopolies, namely Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft.

Internet infrastructure policy is increasingly a topic of discussion in military strategy and policy decision-making

title: How Cambodia’s law on ‘freedom parks’ curtailed people’s right to protest
content:
Only one freedom park has been identified in the country

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Participants hold banners while security officers block them from marching in Phnom Penh during the May 1 Labor Day. Photo from Licadho. CC BY-NC 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Cambodia’s Law on Peaceful Demonstration was supposed to ensure the right of citizens to organize and participate in public assemblies by designating freedom parks in every province. But since its passage in 2009, only one park has been identified, and authorities often impose prohibitions on the use of this space for protests.

As early as 2009, several human rights groups flagged some of the restrictive provisions of the law.
snippet:
Only one freedom park has been identified in the country

title: West-to-east energy, east-to-west computing: The Uyghur costs of China’s digital order
content:
Beijing calls the Uyghur region a ‘national energy and resource strategic security base’

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

The Karamay Cloud Computing Industrial Park of the Uyghur Region. Screenshot from Xinjiang Radio and Television Station. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

On September 14, ministers and senior officials gathered behind closed doors in Urumqi, the capital of China’s Uyghur region, on the eve of the 2026 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Digital Economy Forum. The meeting was presented as a technical and developmental exercise in which participants discussed digital infrastructure, industrial transformation, artificial intelligence, data governance, and the economic value of data. The wider forum was held under the theme “Promoting SCO Data Connectivity, Shaping the Future with AI.”

title: When the right to protest remains, but demonstrating comes at a price
content:
Climate activists are particularly vulnerable to arrest and persecution

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

A climate protest in Copenhagen. Image from Flickr. CC BY-NC-ND 2.0.

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Across Europe, governments are using criminal laws against climate and environmental protesters — a phenomenon that shows few signs of retreating. A comparative study published in late 2025, examining 14 countries across the Global North and South, found that criminalization forms part of a wider pattern of repression. Researchers identified not only arrests, but new anti-protest laws, the strategic use of existing laws and legal processes, surveillance, harassment, and the public vilification of activists.
snippet:
Climate activists are particularly vulnerable to arrest and persecution

title: When telcos shut down the internet, they shut down protests for the government
content:
When the streets become too dangerous, dissent often migrates online

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

A telecom company in Niger. Image via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Room to protest is narrowing across much of the African continent, as governments lean on arrests, curfews, and internet blackouts to blunt dissent. When the streets become too dangerous, dissent often migrates online — which is exactly where telecommunications companies enter the picture, deciding, often under government pressure, whether a phone call gets through or a message reaches its recipient. This piece looks at how that power has been used, and at the accountability telcos have too often avoided.
snippet:
When the streets become too dangerous, dissent often migrates online
